subject: English Language
examFormat: Three papers, all compulsory; Papers 1 and 2 are taken as a composite paper at one sitting. Paper 1: eighty multiple-choice questions (forty lexical, forty structural, options A to D) in 1 hour for 40 marks. Paper 2: essay (50 marks), comprehension (20 marks) and summary (30 marks) in 2 hours for 100 marks. Paper 3 (Nigeria): sixty multiple-choice items on Test of Orals in 45 minutes for 30 marks.
excluded: Paper 1 for Ghana only (including its literature section), and the Listening Comprehension Test for Ghana, The Gambia and Sierra Leone, because they do not apply to Nigeria. Preamble, aims and scheme of examination summarised in examFormat.

topics.name: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
objectives: Use and understand the vocabulary of everyday usage (home, social relationships and common core school subjects)
Use the general vocabulary associated with the listed fields of human activity
Respond to sense relations in the use of lexical items, e.g. synonyms, antonyms and homonyms
topics.content: Questions test the vocabulary of everyday usage (home, social relationships and common core school subjects) and the general vocabulary of these fields: building and building construction; agriculture; fishing; stock exchange; health; environment; culture, institutions and ceremonies; law and order; motor vehicles and travelling; government and administration; sports; religion; science and technology; animal husbandry; advertising; human internal body system and function. 'General' vocabulary means words generally known, used and understood by most educated people who are not engaged in the field but may read, speak or write about it (e.g. 'pedestrian bridge' and 'traffic signs' but not specialised terms like 'berm' or 'camber'). Items test use and understanding of the lexis rather than dictionary definitions, exploring sense relations such as synonyms, antonyms and homonyms.

topics.name: Idioms and Collocations
objectives: Interpret idiomatic expressions and collocations whose total meaning cannot be arrived at from the dictionary meanings of the individual words
topics.content: Idiomatic expressions and collocations, e.g. 'hook, line and sinker' and 'every Tom, Dick and Harry'.

topics.name: Structural Elements of English (Lexis Section)
objectives: Apply the sequence of tenses correctly
Match pronouns with their antecedents
Use prepositions correctly
topics.content: Structural elements of English such as sequence of tenses, matching of pronouns with their antecedents and correct use of prepositions.

topics.name: Figurative Usage
objectives: Recognise when an expression is used figuratively and not only when it is used literally

topics.name: Structure
objectives: Recognise patterns of changes in word-forms which indicate number, tense, degree, etc.
Recognise the patterns in which different categories of words regularly combine to form groups, and groups combine to form sentences
Use structural words such as conjunctions, determiners and prepositions

topics.name: Essay Writing
objectives: Communicate effectively in writing in a letter
Communicate effectively in writing a speech
Write narration
Write description
Write argument/debate
Write a report
Write an article
Write exposition
Write creative pieces
topics.content: Section A of Paper 2 (50 marks, about 50 minutes): five questions, of which one is answered. Topics demand letter, speech, narration, description, argument/debate, report, article, exposition and creative writing. Marks are awarded for content (relevance of ideas to the topic); organization (formal features where applicable, good paragraphing, appropriate emphasis and arrangement of ideas); expression (effective control of vocabulary and sentence structure); and mechanical accuracy (correct grammar, punctuation, spelling, etc.). The minimum length is 450 words.

topics.name: Comprehension
objectives: Find appropriate equivalents for selected words or phrases
Understand the factual content of a passage
Make inferences from the content of the passage
Understand the use of English expressions that reveal or reflect sentiments, emotions and attitudes
Identify and label basic grammatical structures, words, phrases or clauses and explain their functions in context
Identify and explain basic literary terms and expressions
Recast phrases or sentences into grammatical alternatives
topics.content: Section B of Paper 2 (20 marks, about 30 minutes): one passage of at least 350 words, all questions answered. The passage is drawn from a wide variety of sources, written in modern English within the experience of candidates. The test includes at least four questions on understanding the factual content.

topics.name: Summary
objectives: Extract relevant information from a passage
Summarise the points demanded in clear, concise English, avoiding repetition and redundancy
Present a summary of specific aspects or portions of a passage
topics.content: Section C of Paper 2 (30 marks, about 40 minutes): one prose passage of about 500 words, selected from a wide variety of suitable sources including excerpts from narratives, dialogues and expositions of social, cultural, economic and political issues in any part of the world.

topics.name: Oral English: Test of Orals
objectives: Recognise vowels (pure vowels and diphthongs)
Recognise consonants and consonant clusters
Recognise rhymes
Identify word stress and syllable structure
Identify emphatic stress and intonation patterns
Use phonetic symbols
topics.content: Paper 3 for Nigeria: sixty multiple-choice questions covering vowels (pure vowels and diphthongs); consonants and clusters; rhymes; word stress/syllable structure; emphatic stress/intonation patterns; and phonetic symbols.

subtopics.name: Consonants
objectives: Recognise and produce all significant sound contrasts in the consonantal system of English (initial, medial and final), e.g. they/day, ship/chip, fan/van, pit/fit, pit/bit, tuck/duck, card/guard, gear/jeer, buzzes/buses, boat/both, cup/cub

Recognise and produce consonant clusters occurring initially and finally in a syllable, and the consonant sounds in a cluster in the right order, e.g. play/pray, sting/string, three/tree, rains/range, sent/send, nest/next, ask/axe

subtopics.name: Vowels
objectives: Recognise and produce all significant sound contrasts in the vowel system of English: pure vowels, diphthongs and triphthongs, e.g. seat/sit, sit/set, peck/pack, pack/park, cart/cat, load/lord, pool/pull/pole

subtopics.name: Stress
objectives: Contrast stressed and unstressed syllables in words, and recognise shifting of stress in different derivations of the same word with consequent change in vowel quality, e.g. 'increase (noun) and in'crease (verb)

Recognise that English is a stress-timed language, and that in most sentences only nouns, main verbs, adjectives and adverbs are stressed (final, relative and possessive pronouns are not stressed unless contrast is intended)
Recognise strong and weak forms of words that are pronounced differently depending on whether they are stressed in the sentence
Recognise the use of emphatic stress, most commonly to indicate a contrast, realised partly as a change in pitch within the intonation pattern

subtopics.name: Intonation
objectives: Recognise the different forms English intonation takes in relation to grammar and the attitudes conveyed by the speaker
Identify the falling pattern (statements, WH-questions, commands) and the rising pattern (yes/no questions, incomplete utterances, questions in statement form)
Recognise that placing the changing pitch elsewhere than on the last stressed syllable implies a contrast to the item on which it falls
